title: Identification and degrees of freedom
summary: A CB-SEM model is identified when its parameters can be recovered uniquely from the covariances; counting moments and parameters gives the degrees of freedom that make fit testable.

body.text: A model is identified if only one set of parameter values reproduces its implied covariance matrix ([[identification]]). A necessary condition is that the number of free parameters t does not exceed the number of distinct variances and covariances of p indicators.

body.explanation: p(p + 1)/2 is the number of distinct variances and covariances of p indicators; t is the number of free parameters. df < 0: not identified; df = 0: just identified; df > 0: over-identified and testable.

body.text: Every factor also needs a scale. With a [[marker-variable]] the first loading is fixed to 1; with a [[fixed-factor-variance]] (std-lv) the factor variance is fixed to 1. Both give the same fit and the same standardised solution. One factor needs at least three indicators to be identified on its own; two-indicator factors are identified only through their correlations with other factors (Bollen 1989).

In the two-factor example p = 8: 36 moments, 17 parameters (8 loadings, 8 unique variances, 1 factor correlation under std-lv), so df = 19. A one-factor model with three indicators has df = 0: it reproduces the data perfectly whatever they are, so its fit says nothing.

mistake.title: Celebrating perfect fit with df = 0
mistake.text: A just-identified model has χ² = 0 and "perfect" fit indices by construction. SEM Studio warns about this; the model may still be wrong, and you cannot tell from its fit.

tryIt.task: Run CB-SEM on this one-factor model with five indicators and check df = 5. Then switch the identification between marker and std-lv on the Analysis page and compare χ² and the standardised loadings.

checks.question: A one-factor model with 6 indicators, identified by fixing the factor variance to 1. What are the degrees of freedom?

options.feedback: Correct: 6 × 7 / 2 = 21 moments; 6 loadings + 6 unique variances = 12 parameters; 21 − 12 = 9.
That is the number of covariances without the variances; the moments include the 6 variances too.
With std-lv the factor variance is fixed, not estimated, so there are 12 free parameters, not 13.

checks.question: What changes when you switch from marker to std-lv identification?

options.text: Only the unstandardised scale of the factors; χ², df and the standardised solution stay the same.
options.feedback: Correct. They are two scalings of the same model.

options.text: The fit, because a different parameter is fixed.
options.feedback: Both choices fix exactly one scale per factor; fit is identical.
Standardised loadings do not depend on the scaling choice.

checks.explanation: Scaling is arbitrary; fit is not affected.
